newsitem.title: USA: Great value in G11 bonds hard to find-US fund mngr.
newsitem.headline: Great value in G11 bonds hard to find-US fund mngr.

text.p: Prospects for higher global interest rates makes finding exceptional value in bonds of major nations a challenge, said F. Mark Turner, newly appointed Chief Investment Officer of global bond products at Schooner Asset Management Co, an affiliate of Schooner Capital Corp.

"I would argue that in the (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, and Group of 11) markets, it is tough to find really exceptional value, especially at the front end of the curve," said Turner.
Turner defined G11 as G7 members plus Austria, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Spain.

Schooner Asset Management announced on Wednesday that Turner will join the firm after two years as senior portfolio manager at the investment management affiliate of France's Caisse des Depots et Consignations in New York.
"We would be extremely cautious in taking on huge amounts of duration anywhere in the world at this point," he added, speaking to investors and the press in a conference call.

Turner said the popular so-called "convergence play" of investing in high-yield European bond markets such as Spain and Italy ahead of Europe's 1999 deadline for a single currency was mostly tapped out.
"There is clearly not a huge amount of upside and potentially I would argue there is some downside in the longer run," he said.

Turner forecast U.S. Federal Reserve policymakers will raise the federal funds rate target at least 50 basis points by yearend and possibly another 100 basis points before the peak of the current tightening cycle.
The Fed raised the federal funds rate target 25 basis points to 5.5 percent at its March 25 meeting, the first rate rise in more than two years.
Turner also predicted the benchmark 30-year long bond yield will reach a "high 7.0 percent" by yearend and "easily" hit 8.0 to 10 percent by the end of the cycle.

"It's our contention the Federal Reserve will continue to tighten monetary policy this year and that as early as the third quarter, we will see a change in the stance of the Bank of Japan and possibly the Bundesbank in the latter part of this year -- providing a backdrop for fixed income securities in a cyclical sense which will be somewhat unpropitious," Turner said.
He said the U.S. tightening cycle could be exaccerbated if the Fed does not start acting more proactively.
"One difference between '87, '94 and now is at least in those cycles the Fed seemed to be somewhat ahead of the curve. This time, they were clearly behind it," Turner said.
"If they remain behind it for the first part of the tightening cycle, then it could go much further," he said, adding that despite the March rate hike, Fed policy was still "behind the curve".
Lincoln Rathnam, President of Schooner Asset Management, said decent rates of return in fixed income can still be made, especially in emerging markets.
"Respectable rates of return can be obtained from a combination of currency stability, with eventual pressure to depreciate, and high short-term rates," Rathnam said.
Rathnam and Turner first collaborated in 1989 when they launched the industry's first sovereign emerging markets bond fund.
